title: Sweden's SEK 44m bet365 Fine: Deposit Limit Lessons
excerpt: Spelinspektionen's reported SEK 44m sanction shows Sweden will treat optional or nominal deposit limits as a systemic breach.
paras: Reports published on 16 October 2026 indicate that Spelinspektionen, the Swedish Gambling Authority, has imposed combined sanctions of SEK 44 million on the Hillside entities that operate bet365 in Sweden, split between SEK 40 million for the sports entity and SEK 4 million for the gaming entity. The conduct under review ran from 1 January 2019 to 19 April 2022, and the authority concluded that the breaches concerned customer care and deposit-limit obligations under the Gambling Act. Operators should read the decision as a statement of regulatory method as much as a penalty.

The central finding, as reported, is that players were able to choose to play without a deposit limit. Rather than setting a numerical limit that players had to actively raise, bet365 is said to have relied on what it described as a hidden technical limit of SEK 500 million. Spelinspektionen's position, consistent with its published guidance, is that a limit which no ordinary player could ever reach does not discharge the obligation to give players a meaningful tool for controlling their own spending. A cap that exists in the system architecture but not in the player's decision-making is, in substance, no cap at all.

The authority also characterised the failings as systematic and serious enough to justify a licence review, potentially including revocation. That the sanction stopped at a fine and compliance guidance is attributed to corrective action taken by the operator during the audit. This is the practical takeaway for licensees: remediation that is genuine, timely and demonstrable during an inspection remains the single most influential mitigating factor in Swedish enforcement, and can be the difference between a financial penalty and the loss of a licence.

The retrospective nature of the case deserves attention. The period examined ended more than four years ago, yet the sanction was set by reference to current regulatory expectations on customer care and the authority's present enforcement posture. Swedish law allows a sanction fee to be calculated by reference to turnover, and there is no suggestion that a long gap between the breach and the decision reduces exposure. Operators that have since changed their journeys should still expect historical conduct to be reviewed if it surfaces in an audit, a complaint or a licence renewal.

For compliance teams, the immediate work is a gap analysis of every limit-setting flow. Is a deposit limit mandatory at registration, or can it be skipped? Is the default a number the average player would recognise as restrictive? Are increases subject to a cooling-off period, and are decreases applied immediately? Are limits applied consistently across product verticals and across entities that share a customer? Where a group runs separate sports and gaming licences, the case is a reminder that each licensed entity carries its own liability and its own sanction.

Contracts and governance deserve equal attention. Platform and B2B suppliers that configure limit mechanics on behalf of operators should expect operators to seek warranties, audit rights and indemnities tied to Spelinspektionen's published interpretation. Boards should receive regular reporting on customer-care metrics and on any divergence between configured limits and observed player behaviour. Where a technical default is later found to be non-compliant, documenting the date it was identified and the date it was fixed will materially affect how the authority views cooperation.

The wider context is a Nordic and European convergence on affordability and limit-setting. Regulators in the Netherlands, Denmark, Finland and the United Kingdom are each tightening expectations that safer-gambling tools are effective rather than merely present. Operators with multi-market licences should treat the Swedish position as a benchmark and align their strictest standard across all regulated markets, rather than maintaining jurisdiction-specific patches that are costly to audit. Specialist Swedish counsel should be engaged early where an inspection letter arrives.

title: AGCO's $200k theScore Bet Penalty: Cash-Out Offers
excerpt: The AGCO fined theScore Bet its maximum $200,000 after two cash-out offers on a parlay were never honoured.
paras: On 6 October 2026 the Alcohol and Gaming Commission of Ontario announced a $200,000 monetary penalty against Score Media and Gaming Inc., the operator of theScore Bet. The amount is the maximum the Registrar can impose for a single breach of the Registrar's Standards for Internet Gaming, and the decision is notable because it addresses not what happened to a bet but how an offer was presented to a player.

According to reports, the case arose from a $1,000 multi-leg parlay placed on 14 March 2025 across NHL, NBA and NCAA basketball games. The player was shown a cash-out offer of about $380,000, accepted it, and saw the transaction rejected by automated verification after the odds moved. A second offer of roughly $100,000 was presented four minutes later, accepted, and again failed to complete. The final leg then lost and the player received nothing. The Registrar found that neither offer was achievable as presented to the player.

The legal reasoning matters more than the facts. The Registrar did not need to find that the operator acted dishonestly or that the outcome was unfair on the odds. The breach lay in displaying an offer that the platform could not or would not honour, which the Registrar treated as incompatible with the standards on fair and transparent play. For operators, the lesson is that every price shown to a player is a representation, and a system that can display a price that its own back end will reject creates regulatory exposure independent of any contractual argument.

This is the fourth AGCO penalty against an iGaming registrant since early August 2026, following reported penalties against Betty Gaming, Booming Games and NorthStar Gaming, and the second for theScore Bet in twelve months after a $105,000 penalty in October 2025 relating to a high-risk player. Repeat findings against the same registrant rarely go unremarked. Operators with a history of penalties should expect closer scrutiny at renewal and should prepare for the possibility that prior matters will be cited as aggravating context.

Operationally, the case points to a design problem that is common in live-odds products. Cash-out values are computed continuously, whereas acceptance involves latency, validation and a re-pricing check. Where the displayed value and the validated value can diverge, operators need a clear rule: either lock the offer for a defined window, or re-quote explicitly and require a fresh acceptance. Silent rejection after the player has pressed accept, particularly without immediate and plain-language messaging, is the pattern most likely to attract regulatory attention.

Procedurally, theScore Bet has 15 days to request a hearing before the Licence Appeal Tribunal, which means the penalty is not necessarily final. The AGCO did not order compensation to the player, and the public record does not confirm whether the customer was reimbursed. Ontario's framework treats monetary penalties as regulatory rather than compensatory, so affected players may need to pursue separate civil or complaint routes, a point operators should factor into their complaint-handling and dispute-resolution procedures.

Practical steps for Ontario registrants include auditing the cash-out and bet-acceptance flows for any state in which a displayed price can be rejected, logging every offer, acceptance and rejection with timestamps, training customer support to escalate such events immediately, and testing the user interface for clear failure messaging. Operators should also review their terms for any reservation of rights on cash-out values and confirm that those terms are consistent with the standards, because the Registrar is unlikely to treat small-print as a defence to a misleading on-screen price.

title: HMRC RGD Receipts at 40%: The Yield Debate
excerpt: Provisional HMRC figures show Remote Gaming Duty at 40% yielding £376m for April-June 2026, fuelling the Budget fight over rates.
paras: HMRC's provisional statistics for April to June 2026 give the first quarter of evidence on the 40% rate of Remote Gaming Duty, which replaced the earlier 21% rate on 1 April 2026. Receipts were reported at £376 million, up £67 million or 22% on the same quarter of 2025, but below the £360 million collected in the first quarter of 2026 when the lower rate still applied. Machine Games Duty receipts were £162 million for the quarter, about 5% higher than a year earlier.

Read carefully, those numbers support both sides of the policy argument. Treasury supporters can point to a year-on-year increase and to the fact that the headline rate has nearly doubled without a collapse in receipts. Industry bodies point out that a 19-point increase in the rate would be expected to raise far more than 22% if gross gaming yield were stable, and that quarter-on-quarter receipts under the 40% rate are not clearly ahead of those under the 21% rate once seasonality is considered. Neither reading is conclusive after a single quarter, and the full behavioural response may not yet be visible.

Operators are reported to be mitigating through reduced bonusing, tighter VIP economics, lower marketing budgets and, in some cases, product-level changes that shift players between duty categories. The Netherlands is frequently cited by the industry as a cautionary comparison, where duty increases in 2025 are said to have raised a small fraction of the revenue originally forecast. Whether the UK will follow a similar path depends on player migration to unlicensed offerings, which is difficult to measure in any official series but which the Gambling Commission treats as a live enforcement concern.

The political backdrop is the autumn Budget scheduled for 28 October 2026. The November 2025 Budget had already legislated an increase in General Betting Duty from 15% to 25% from April 2027 for remote betting and abolished Bingo Duty, and commentary now centres on Machine Games Duty, where a doubling of rates is widely rumoured though not confirmed. Land-based casino and betting-shop groups are campaigning that such a rise would put planned investment and shop estates at risk, while advocates of higher taxation argue that the industry can bear greater contributions to public finances and harm-related costs.

For operators, the practical question is how to plan under uncertainty. Finance teams should run scenarios for the existing 40% RGD rate, the legislated 25% remote betting duty from April 2027, and a range of possible MGD outcomes, and should test covenant headroom and licence-fee budgets against each. The recent increase in Gambling Commission licence fees, which operators must also absorb, compounds the pressure and narrows the margin for error in lower-yield segments.

Contractual consequences deserve early attention. Affiliate agreements, revenue-share arrangements with B2B suppliers and white-label contracts commonly define revenue by reference to net gaming revenue after duty, and a change in rate can shift economics between parties without any breach. Change-in-law clauses, price-review mechanisms and termination rights should be reviewed now so that renegotiation, if needed, happens before a Budget announcement rather than after it.

The enduring lesson of the HMRC data is that duty policy has moved from a stable background assumption to an active risk factor for every UK-facing business. Boards should expect to receive tax-sensitivity analysis alongside compliance reporting, and counsel advising on UK market entry, financing or acquisitions should ensure that diligence covers the duty position by product line rather than relying on group-level effective rates. Specialist tax advice should be taken before the Budget statement and again once its detail is published.

title: YouTube Masthead Opens to Gambling Ads: Compliance
excerpt: Google will let licensed gambling advertisers buy YouTube Masthead placements from 21 October, raising fresh duties for operators.
paras: Reports dated 9 October 2026 state that Google is updating its policies so that online gambling advertisers will be able to run YouTube Masthead campaigns from 21 October. The Masthead is the premium placement at the top of the YouTube homepage, typically the first thing a viewer sees, and it has until now been unavailable to gambling advertisers. Eligibility remains subject to Google's Gambling and games policy and to the advertiser holding the relevant licence or certification in each area where the ad is shown.

The change arrives at an awkward regulatory moment. Campaigns against gambling advertising are intensifying in the United Kingdom, Australia and the United States, and legislators in several markets are weighing restrictions on broadcast and online exposure. A placement that reaches a very large and indiscriminate audience in a single impression is exactly the kind of format that regulators scrutinise for exposure to minors and vulnerable adults. Operators that are legally entitled to buy the format should not assume that it is prudent or low-risk to do so.

In Great Britain, the relevant standards are the CAP and BCAP rules enforced by the Advertising Standards Authority, together with licence conditions on advertising and social responsibility set by the Gambling Commission. An ad must not appeal strongly to under-18s, must not be targeted at them, and must be placed in media where at least 75% of the audience is estimated to be over 18. The Masthead, which is served on the logged-out homepage as well as to signed-in users, makes audience composition harder to evidence than age-gated or audience-segmented formats, and operators will need to document the basis for their assumptions.

Geographic targeting is the second major issue. Google's policy ties approval to licensing in each targeted location, so a campaign that spills into a jurisdiction where the operator is not licensed risks both a platform sanction and an illegal-advertising allegation under local law. This is particularly relevant in the United States, where permissibility differs by state, in Australia, where the Interactive Gambling Act and the code of advertising restrictions apply, and across the European Union, where national rules on advertising range from permissive to near-total bans.

Liability also reaches beyond the operator. Media agencies, affiliates and creative vendors who buy or produce the placement may be considered responsible persons under local advertising codes, and several regulators have signalled willingness to pursue them. Insertion orders and agency agreements should allocate responsibility for targeting, age-audience evidence, creative approval and takedown, with a short escalation route for regulator or platform complaints and an obligation to preserve campaign logs.

A related point is the contrast drawn in the trade press between Google's expansion and the pressure on Meta over illegal gambling advertising. Platforms are being asked to police advertiser eligibility, and national regulators are increasingly willing to rely on platform-level controls as evidence of compliance. Operators should keep their own licence documentation current and in a form that can be submitted to platforms rapidly, because delays in verification are as likely to disrupt a campaign as any substantive refusal.

The sensible approach is to treat the Masthead as a high-risk placement requiring a formal sign-off. A pre-campaign checklist should confirm licences for each target territory, review creative against the applicable code, set frequency and time-of-day limits, exclude sensitive audiences where the platform allows it, and nominate a person with authority to pause the campaign immediately. Specialist advertising counsel in each target market should review the plan before the format goes live.

title: Duty-of-Care Fines: France ANJ and Singapore GRA
excerpt: Fines in France and Singapore show regulators now test whether safeguards work in practice, not whether they exist on paper.
paras: Two recent sanctions in different regions show a common regulatory theme: safer-gambling systems are being judged by outcomes. In France, the Autorité Nationale des Jeux reported in July 2026 a sanction of about $572,000 against an unnamed licensed operator for failures in its duty of care. In Singapore, the Gambling Regulatory Authority disclosed in its annual report, released on 6 October 2026, fines totalling S$275,000 against Singapore Pools, Marina Bay Sands and Resorts World Sentosa. The facts differ, but the supervisory logic is the same.

The French case concerned the identification of at-risk players. The ANJ reviewed the activity of 30 players between October 2023 and March 2024 against seven criteria drawn from its prevention framework, and found that 23 had been wrongly rated as low risk and six were missed entirely. The operator disputes the decision, arguing that French law does not clearly define excessive or pathological gambling, and has two months to file an administrative appeal. Whatever the outcome, the regulator has signalled that it will assess the quality of risk models by testing them against real player histories.

The Singapore decisions turned on process failures. Singapore Pools was fined S$100,000 after a system flaw meant that updating identification documents did not re-check exclusion status, allowing a self-excluded person to place bets; the operator found the lapse itself in April 2024, suspended the account within 30 minutes and reported it. Marina Bay Sands was fined S$100,000 for offering promotional chances through its non-gaming membership, tied to casino activity, without the prior approval required for casino promotions between 2018 and 2023. Resorts World Sentosa was fined S$75,000 because membership tiers were incorrectly maintained and the approved programme did not run as approved.

Separately, the Auditor-General's Office reported that between 2023 and 2025, 120 people under exclusion orders were admitted to the two casinos and 79 Singapore Pools accounts held by excluded persons were not closed. Those findings are described as unrelated to the GRA fines, and the authorities say the errors were fixed by February 2026. The pairing of annual-report fines with an independent audit shows that operators face parallel scrutiny from more than one body.

The comparison with Europe is instructive. Sweden's recent SEK 44 million sanction concerned deposit limits that were nominal rather than effective, and the United Kingdom's Gambling Commission has repeatedly emphasised that customer-interaction triggers must lead to action. In each system, the regulator asks whether controls were designed to work, whether they were tested, and whether the operator found and reported failures promptly. Self-detection and swift remediation, as in the Singapore Pools matter, reduced but did not eliminate the penalty.

For operators, three practical conclusions follow. First, change management is a compliance control: any system update, including a simple change to identity data, should be tested for its effect on exclusion, limit and risk-flag logic. Second, risk models should be back-tested against sample player histories and the results retained, so that a regulator's sampling exercise can be answered with evidence. Third, promotional and membership schemes in licensed venues should be mapped against the approvals actually granted, with periodic reconciliation of live configuration to approved terms.

Legal teams should also consider the dispute dimension. Where a statutory definition is open-textured, as the French operator argues, the better course is to document the operator's own interpretation, the evidence supporting it and its alignment with regulatory guidance well before an inspection. Counsel should be involved early when a sampling exercise or audit letter arrives, because the framing of the first response often shapes the sanction analysis and any later appeal.
